title: Week 1 assignment: Comparing protein extraction protocols
text:
Study description
A laboratory wants to compare a standard protein extraction protocol with a modified protocol. The aim is to determine whether the modified protocol increases protein yield while accounting for differences between tissue donors.
Tissue from each of ten donors is divided into eight aliquots. Within each donor, four aliquots are randomly assigned to the standard protocol and four to the modified protocol. Each aliquot undergoes its assigned extraction protocol and is measured once, giving 80 observations.
The outcome is protein yield, measured in micrograms of extracted protein per milligram of tissue (µg/mg). Larger values indicate a higher yield. These are simulated teaching data.


Dataset
Each row represents one tissue aliquot.



Variable
Description




aliquot
Unique identifier for the aliquot


donor
Tissue donor, labelled Donor 01 to Donor 10


protocol
Extraction protocol: Standard or Modified


protein_yield
Protein yield in µg/mg





Analysis tasks

Describe the design. Identify the experimental unit and blocking variable, and explain how the protocols were assigned within donors.
Explore the data. Create a plot showing individual protein yields, protocol-specific means within each donor, and overall protocol means. Discuss whether the plot suggests substantial differences between donors, considering both the donor-specific means and the variation among aliquots within donors.
Fit a random-intercept model. Include protocol as a fixed effect and a random intercept for donor. Use dummy coding for protocol, with Standard as the reference. Interpret the intercept and protocol coefficient, and explain what the random donor intercept represents.
Interpret the results. Obtain the modified-minus-standard difference, its estimated standard error and its 95% confidence interval. Report and interpret the estimated donor and residual variances. Calculate and interpret the intraclass correlation coefficient.
Check the model and conclude. Examine conditional-residual diagnostic plots and comment on the model assumptions. Write a short conclusion answering the laboratory’s question, including the estimated protocol difference, its uncertainty and appropriate units.

Use the Week 1 labs as references when constructing your analysis. Explain your findings in the context of protein extraction and include units where appropriate.


Report and submission
For this assignment, submit a report created using Quarto that presents your analysis, results and interpretations, using the template provided in the Downloads section below.
The template starts with a setup chunk that uses pak to install the required analysis packages if needed and then loads them. Install pak itself as described in Lab 1 if you have not already done so. The setup chunk runs when you render the document, but its code and output are hidden from the report. Brief instructions for running code and rendering the report are included in the template.
Submit both the completed Quarto source file (.qmd) and the rendered HTML report. Keep your analysis code, results and figures visible in the report, and accompany them with your interpretations. Only the setup chunk is hidden.






NoteHelp with Quarto



For an introduction to creating reports with Quarto, see Chapter 28: Quarto in R for Data Science (2nd edition). It covers text formatting, code chunks, figures, tables and rendering. Chapter 29: Quarto formats provides further information about output formats.

title: Beyond MLR Lab 1: Modeling center as a fixed effect
text:
We return to the rehabilitation trial from the lecture. In this simulated study, 120 patients recovering from knee replacement receive either standard care or an enhanced rehabilitation program. Standard care consists of weekly physiotherapy and home exercises; enhanced care adds a weekly supervised session. The outcome is the distance walked during a six-minute walk test at 12 weeks, measured in meters. A larger distance indicates better walking performance.
The study includes six centers. Within each center, 10 patients are randomly assigned to standard care and 10 to enhanced care. This is a randomized block design, with center as the blocking factor. These are simulated teaching data, not observations from an actual clinical trial.
Our question is: What is the estimated difference in expected walking distance between enhanced and standard care, and how precisely is it estimated? We will explore differences between centers and fit a model that includes center as a fixed effect.
By the end of this lab, you should be able to visualize treatment and center differences, fit and interpret the fixed-effects model, assess the overall contribution of center using an analysis of variance table, and check the model assumptions.






NoteWorking through the lab



Run the code in order in an R script, and record your answers to the questions. The lab page shows the code; you generate the results yourself.

title: Beyond MLR Lab 1: Modeling center as a fixed effect
text:
Use one folder per week
Create a folder for this course, with a separate folder for each week. Keep that week’s lab scripts and data together so that you can find and rerun your analyses when working on the assignment. For Week 1, use the following structure:
BeyondMLR/
  week1/
    lab1.R
    lab2.R
    data/
      rehabilitation_week1.csv
  week2/
Create the week1 folder and its data subfolder now. Download the rehabilitation dataset and save it in week1/data. Keep the filename unchanged.

title: Beyond MLR Lab 1: Modeling center as a fixed effect
section: Save your code in an R script
text:
Save your code in an R script
An R script is a text file with the extension .R that records the commands for your analysis. Saving your code lets you repeat the analysis in a new R session and adapt it later.
In RStudio, select File > New File > R Script and save the file as lab1.R inside week1. Copy the R code from this lab into your script as you work through it. Place the cursor on a line, or select several lines, and click Run to execute them in the Console. The shortcut is Ctrl+Enter on Windows/Linux or Cmd+Enter on macOS. Run the code in order, starting with package loading and data import. RStudio’s code-editing guide describes these controls.
Add comments beginning with # to explain your code and record short answers to the lab questions. Save the script regularly.

title: Beyond MLR Lab 1: Modeling center as a fixed effect
text:
Set the working directory
The working directory is the folder R uses as the starting point for relative file paths. For example, "data/rehabilitation_week1.csv" tells R to look inside the data subfolder of its working directory. Relative paths used to save output also start from this folder.
For this lab, set the working directory to week1, which contains your script and the data folder. Saving or opening a script does not by itself guarantee that R uses that folder as its working directory.






NoteChanging the working directory in RStudio



Select Session > Set Working Directory > Choose Directory…, then choose your week1 folder. Alternatively, with the saved lab1.R script active, select Session > Set Working Directory > To Source File Location.
Run getwd() in the Console to check the selected folder. It should be week1, not its data subfolder. Check this again when starting a new session. These controls are part of RStudio’s working-directory tools.

title: Beyond MLR Lab 1: Modeling center as a fixed effect
text:
Install pak once
An R package provides additional functions, for example for drawing figures or fitting statistical models. Throughout this course, we will use the package manager pak to install the packages we need. It also handles their dependencies: other packages they need to work.
First, install pak itself by running the following command in the Console. You only need to do this once for your current R installation; skip this step if you already have pak installed.

install.packages("pak", repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")

title: Beyond MLR Lab 1: Modeling center as a fixed effect
text:
Use pak throughout the course
Installing a package saves it on your computer. Loading a package makes its functions available in the current R session. Installed packages remain available between sessions, but you need to load them again when you start a new session.
We will follow the same pattern in each lab: load pak with library(pak), use pkg_install() to install the packages needed for that lab, and then load those packages with library(). The pak package manager checks the required packages and their dependencies and keeps already installed versions when they meet the requirements.
For this lab, we need ggplot2 for figures and dplyr for summaries. Add the following code to the beginning of your script and run it. If pak asks whether to proceed, confirm the installation and wait for it to finish.

library(pak)
pkg_install(c("ggplot2", "dplyr"))

Now load the packages for your analysis. Keep these commands in your script so that they run each time you start the lab in a new R session.

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

title: Beyond MLR Lab 1: Modeling center as a fixed effect
text:
Read the data
With week1 as your working directory and the dataset saved in its data subfolder, run the following code. If R cannot find the file, check getwd(), the folder containing the CSV file, and its filename.

rehab <- read.csv("data/rehabilitation_week1.csv")

# Specify the order of the categories explicitly.
rehab$treatment <- factor(rehab$treatment,
                          levels = c("Standard", "Enhanced"))
rehab$center <- factor(rehab$center,
                       levels = paste("Center", LETTERS[1:6]))

head(rehab)
str(rehab)
table(rehab$center, rehab$treatment)

Each row represents one patient. The variables are center, treatment, and distance (six-minute walk distance in meters). A factor tells R that a variable represents categories rather than a continuous measurement. The order of the factor levels will matter when we choose how to represent these categories in the model.






ImportantQuestion 1



Check the allocation table. How many patients are in each treatment group within each center? Why is this allocation useful when comparing the treatments?

title: Beyond MLR Lab 1: Modeling center as a fixed effect
text:
Specify the model
Let \(Y_{ij}\) be the outcome for patient \(i\) in center \(j\), and let \(T_{ij}\) indicate the patient’s treatment. We include an intercept \(\beta_0\), a treatment coefficient \(\beta_1\), and a fixed contribution \(c_j\) for each center:
\[
Y_{ij} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 T_{ij} + c_j + \varepsilon_{ij},
\qquad \varepsilon_{ij} \overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim} N(0,\sigma^2).
\]
Without a constraint, increasing the intercept and decreasing every center contribution by the same amount would leave the model’s predictions unchanged. To define these parameters uniquely, we require the six center contributions to sum to zero:
\[
c_A+c_B+c_C+c_D+c_E+c_F=0.
\]
The model assumes that the expected treatment difference is the same in every center: it contains no treatment-by-center interaction. After accounting for treatment and center, the remaining errors are assumed to be independent and identically distributed Normal variables with mean zero and common variance.
To fit this model in R, we explicitly set how each factor is represented numerically. We use dummy coding for treatment to define \(T_{ij}\) and effects coding for center so that R estimates the center deviations specified above.

title: Beyond MLR Lab 1: Modeling center as a fixed effect
text:
Code treatment using dummy coding
With dummy coding, one category is the reference. We use standard care as the reference and represent treatment by a single indicator:



Treatment
Indicator \(T_{ij}\)




Standard
0


Enhanced
1



Within center \(j\), the expected standard-care outcome is \(\beta_0+c_j\), and the expected enhanced-care outcome is \(\beta_0+\beta_1+c_j\). The treatment coefficient \(\beta_1\) is therefore the enhanced-minus-standard difference.

# The first factor level, Standard, is the reference.
contrasts(rehab$treatment) <- contr.treatment(levels(rehab$treatment))
contrasts(rehab$treatment)

contr.treatment() creates the dummy-coding matrix. Assigning it with contrasts() tells R to use this coding when fitting a model with the treatment factor. Printing the matrix shows how each treatment is represented.

title: Beyond MLR Lab 1: Modeling center as a fixed effect
text:
Code center using effects coding
The sum-to-zero constraint makes each \(c_j\) a deviation from the equally weighted average across centers, comparing patients receiving the same treatment. With standard care coded 0, the intercept \(\beta_0\) is the expected standard-care outcome averaged equally across the six centers. It does not average over the two treatments. In this balanced trial, equal weighting of centers also agrees with weighting by their patient counts.
We use effects coding to estimate these deviations directly. With dummy coding for center instead, the intercept would describe standard care in a reference center, and the other center coefficients would describe differences from that center.

contrasts(rehab$center) <- contr.sum(levels(rehab$center))
contrasts(rehab$center)

contr.sum() creates the effects-coding matrix. Inspect the result: there are six rows, one per center, but only five columns. Centers A–E each have a 1 in their own column and 0 in the others. Center F has \(-1\) in all five columns. Its contribution is therefore minus the sum of the other five contributions; it is not set to zero. Only five center coefficients are needed because the sum-to-zero constraint determines the sixth.
Changing the center coding changes the interpretation of the intercept and center coefficients, but does not change the fitted outcomes or the estimated treatment difference and its standard error. Setting the coding explicitly ensures that the analysis does not depend on previously changed global R options.

title: Beyond MLR Lab 1: Modeling center as a fixed effect
section: Fit the model and read its output
text:
Fit the model and read its output

model_fixed <- lm(distance ~ treatment + center, data = rehab)
summary(model_fixed)

In an R model formula, the outcome is on the left of ~, and predictors are on the right. An intercept is included automatically. R uses the coding we assigned to the treatment and center factors.
In the output, (Intercept) estimates \(\beta_0\), and treatmentEnhanced estimates \(\beta_1\). The five center coefficients are named center1 to center5, corresponding to Centers A–E. For example, a positive center1 indicates a higher expected outcome in Center A than the center average, for either treatment. The model-predicted standard-care outcome in Center A is the intercept plus center1.






ImportantQuestion 3



Interpret the intercept, the treatment coefficient, and center1. How would you recover the contribution for Center F? Why would the intercept have a different interpretation if we used dummy coding for center?

title: Beyond MLR Lab 1: Modeling center as a fixed effect
text:
Treatment effect and uncertainty
In summary(model_fixed), the row treatmentEnhanced gives the estimated enhanced-minus-standard difference, its standard error, and a test against a zero difference. The residual standard error at the bottom of the output estimates the individual-error standard deviation after accounting for treatment and center.
Use confint() to obtain the 95% confidence interval for the treatment coefficient, and sigma() to extract the residual standard deviation.

confint(model_fixed, "treatmentEnhanced")
sigma(model_fixed)

The standard error of the treatment coefficient describes uncertainty about the estimated treatment difference. The residual standard deviation describes the remaining variation in individual walking distances. Both are expressed in meters.






ImportantQuestion 4



What are the estimated enhanced-minus-standard difference, its standard error, and its 95% confidence interval? What is the residual standard deviation, and how does its interpretation differ from that of the treatment coefficient’s standard error?

title: Beyond MLR Lab 1: Modeling center as a fixed effect
text:
Overall contribution of center
The coefficient table describes individual center effects. An analysis of variance (ANOVA) table also provides an overall test of whether expected walking distance differs between centers after accounting for treatment.

anova(model_fixed)

anova() produces a row for treatment, a row for center, and a row for the residual variation.

Df gives the degrees of freedom. Center has five because six center effects are linked by the sum-to-zero constraint.
Sum Sq gives the variation attributed to each term, expressed as a sum of squares.
Mean Sq divides each sum of squares by its degrees of freedom. The residual mean square estimates the individual-error variance.
F value compares a term’s mean square with the residual mean square.
Pr(>F) is the p-value for the corresponding overall test.

For center, the null hypothesis is that expected walking distance is the same in all six centers for patients receiving the same treatment. Under effects coding, this means that all six center effects are zero. The plot and estimated center effects show the size of the differences in meters; the ANOVA table assesses the evidence for those differences.






ImportantQuestion 5



What does the center row tell you about differences between centers after accounting for treatment? Relate this result to the pattern in your exploratory plot.

title: Beyond MLR Lab 2: Modeling center as a random effect
text:
In Lab 1, we analyzed a simulated rehabilitation trial involving 120 patients after knee replacement in six centers. Each center assigned 10 patients to standard care and 10 to enhanced rehabilitation. We fitted a model containing separate fixed center effects.
We now keep the same randomized block design and the same question: What is the difference in expected six-minute walk distance at 12 weeks between enhanced and standard care, and how precisely is it estimated? Instead of estimating separate fixed center parameters, we describe center contributions using a distribution. This also allows us to quantify variation between centers.
By the end of this lab, you should be able to fit a random-intercept model, interpret its treatment estimate and uncertainty, interpret its variance components and intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC), and assess its conditional residuals.

title: Beyond MLR Lab 2: Modeling center as a random effect
text:
Extract the variances
VarCorr() returns the estimated variance components. Converting its output to a data frame makes it straightforward to use the values in a calculation.

variance_components <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(model_random))
variance_components

center_variance <- variance_components$vcov[
  variance_components$grp == "center"
]
patient_variance <- variance_components$vcov[
  variance_components$grp == "Residual"
]

c(center_variance = center_variance,
  patient_variance = patient_variance)

The vcov column contains variances; the sdcor column contains their standard deviations for this model. Use the variances, not the standard deviations, in the intraclass correlation coefficient calculation.

title: Beyond MLR Lab 2: Modeling center as a random effect
text:
Introduce the intraclass correlation
After accounting for treatment, the remaining outcome variation consists of the shared center contribution and the individual error:
\[
u_{ij}=c_j+\varepsilon_{ij},
\qquad \operatorname{Var}(u_{ij})=\sigma_c^2+\sigma^2.
\]
For two different patients in the same center, the shared center contribution gives
\[
\operatorname{Cov}(u_{ij},u_{kj})=\sigma_c^2 \quad (i\ne k).
\]
Dividing this covariance by the common variance gives the intraclass correlation coefficient:
\[
\mathrm{ICC}=\frac{\sigma_c^2}{\sigma_c^2+\sigma^2}.
\]
This has two connected interpretations:

The proportion of outcome variance remaining after accounting for treatment that is attributable to differences between centers.
The correlation between outcomes of two different patients in the same center, after accounting for their treatments and averaging over the modeled center distribution.

If we condition on a particular center effect as well as treatment, only the independent individual errors remain. The within-center correlation above arises because patients share a random center contribution.

icc <- center_variance / (center_variance + patient_variance)
icc







ImportantQuestion 3



Calculate the intraclass correlation coefficient. Interpret it both as a variance proportion and as a within-center correlation. What correlation does the model assume for patients in different centers, after accounting for treatment?
